question: Which statement best describes The render pipeline?
options: Reflow (layout) recomputes geometry and is the most expensive — triggered by changing width, height, top/left, font-size, or reading offsetWidth. Repaint fills pixels again without re-layout — triggered by changing color, background, box-shadow, or visibility. Composite-only changes (transform, opacity) skip layout and paint entirely and run on the GPU — the cheapest. Aim to stay in the composite stage for animation.

After the DOM and CSSOM are built, the browser runs a pixel pipeline: Style (compute which rules apply and resolve values), Layout (compute geometry — sizes and positions), Paint (fill in pixels for text, colors, borders, shadows into layers), and Composite (assemble layers on the GPU). Each stage feeds the next, so changes high in the pipeline (layout) force everything below it to rerun.

Animating layout properties (left, top, width, margin) triggers reflow + repaint every frame, often dropping below 60fps. transform (translate/scale/rotate) and opacity can be handled entirely by the compositor on a separate layer, so they animate smoothly without touching layout or paint. The rule of thumb: animate transform and opacity, not geometry.

will-change hints to the browser that a property is about to animate, letting it promote the element to its own compositor layer ahead of time and avoid a first-frame hitch. It's powerful but must be used sparingly — too many promoted layers consume memory and can hurt performance. Apply it just before animating and remove it after, never as a blanket rule.

The old advice to avoid the universal selector or descendant selectors for speed is largely outdated. Modern engines match selectors right-to-left and style recalculation is rarely the bottleneck for typical pages. The real wins are reducing the amount of CSS, avoiding huge style recalcs on big DOM trees, and not triggering layout — not micro-optimizing individual selectors.

question: Which statement best describes Selector performance: myth vs reality?
options: content-visibility: auto tells the browser to skip rendering work (layout and paint) for off-screen content until it scrolls near the viewport, dramatically cutting initial render cost for long pages. Pair it with contain-intrinsic-size so the scrollbar and layout don't jump as content is realized. It's one of the highest-leverage modern CSS performance features.

Critical CSS is the minimal set of styles needed to render above-the-fold content, inlined into the HTML <head> so the first paint isn't blocked on an external stylesheet round-trip. The rest of the CSS loads asynchronously. This improves First Contentful Paint and Largest Contentful Paint, especially on slow connections, at the cost of build complexity.
